name: PT Victoria Investama Tbk

frontmatter.title: Victoria Investama: a financial conglomerate priced for an earning power it has not shown
frontmatter.summary: VICO is a small Indonesian financial holding company whose equity is mostly one bank that earns little on a large capital base. We initiate at SELL with a Rp66 target, -49.6% from Rp137. Our base case assumes a mid-single-digit sustainable return on equity against the 9.5% the price implies. The launch dividend and the larger bank stake are welcome but do not close that gap; liquidity is the binding constraint on both sides.
thesis: The profit jump is a disposal gain: the sale of Bank Victoria Syariah to BTN added IDR532.8bn of pre-tax gain, and ex-gain the group earned a low-single-digit return on equity [S2].
One bank is the group: the bank segment result is IDR429.3bn of IDR455.8bn total segment result, and Bank Victoria is most of the IDR1,845.9bn minority interest [S2].
Justified P/BV on a 5.4% sustainable ROE, a 13.9% cost of equity and 4.0% terminal growth is 0.15x of book, or Rp36 a share [S2][S10].

The IDR121.7bn dividend approved at the special meeting of 18 September 2026 is real cash, but the dividend-discount cross-check values the shares at Rp40 because the payout is thin and the cost of equity high [S10].
The share price implies a 9.5% sustainable ROE; no year in the last four audited accounts comes close to that [S2].

catalysts.event: Q4-2026 and full-year quarterly filing: the bank's credit cost, non-performing loans and capital ratios, and parent-level cash after the disposal proceeds
FY2026 audited accounts, the first clean year after the Syariah exit: the test of whether normalised return on equity is really improving
Annual general meeting: dividend policy on FY2026 profit and any further Bank Victoria share purchases funded by the disposal proceeds
OJK fit-and-proper decision on the President Director handover recorded by the June annual meeting

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Victoria Investama at SELL with a target of Rp66, -49.6% below the Rp137 last traded, before the Rp3 of dividend we expect over the next twelve months. VICO is not an operating company. It is a holding company for a set of small Indonesian financial businesses, of which one, Bank Victoria International, is most of the balance sheet and almost all of the profit. The holding company's own equity has grown faster than its earnings capacity, and the result is a group that earns a return on equity well below the return its shareholders should demand [S2].

The reported numbers look far better than the business. FY2025 attributable profit of IDR474.0bn carries IDR532.8bn of pre-tax gain on the sale of the group's Syariah bank to Bank Tabungan Negara, a transaction that closed in June 2025 [S2]. Strip that out and the group earned roughly a fifth of the reported figure, which is the same order of magnitude as FY2023 and FY2024 [S2]. The trailing twelve months to September 2026 show a modest improvement in the underlying run-rate, and our forecast for FY2026 is IDR188.7bn [S2][S0].

Our variant view is not that the company is badly run. It is that the market is paying for an earning power the group has not demonstrated. At Rp137 the shares change hands at 0.5x our FY2026 book value and at 11.0x our FY2026 earnings. For a bank-heavy balance sheet priced at a discount to book, that looks modest until the return on that book is considered: the price is consistent with a sustainable return on equity near 9.5%, roughly double what the accounts show [S2]. Three things move our value: the return Bank Victoria earns on its capital, the share of profit the holding company pays out, and the discount the market applies to an illiquid, tightly held holding company [S2][S10].

The bull case is real and we present it honestly in section five. The group has just bought more of its bank at a price below book, it has a fresh capital base after the Syariah sale, and it has started paying dividends from the proceeds [S4][S10]. If Bank Victoria's credit costs normalise and its return on equity moves into double digits, the justified multiple on the group's book rises quickly. We do not think the evidence supports that yet, and the price already assumes a good part of it.
What the company is

PT Victoria Investama is an Indonesian investment company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange. It began as a securities firm and has been built into a financial-services group with seven reportable segments: consulting services, securities underwriting and brokerage, loss insurance, investment management, life insurance and banking, plus the holding company itself [S2]. The annual report describes the group as providing corporate finance and advisory services, securities trading and underwriting, general and life insurance, asset management and conventional and sharia banking [S5]. The company was renamed Victoria Investama in 2012 and is headquartered in South Jakarta [S0].

The most important structural fact is that VICO has been designated by the financial services authority as a non-operating financial conglomerate holding company under the conglomerate regulation that took effect in 2024 [S6]. That status changes the company's articles and its purpose: it is now formally the parent of a regulated financial group rather than an operating securities house with side businesses [S6]. It also means the group's capital and governance are supervised at the consolidated level, which is the right lens for a shareholder.
Segments and where the money comes from

The mix is lopsided. In FY2025 the bank segment produced IDR955.3bn of revenue from external parties out of IDR1,056.7bn of total operating revenue, and a segment result of IDR429.3bn out of IDR455.8bn for the group [S2]. The remaining segments are small: loss insurance contributed IDR14.0bn of segment result, investment management lost IDR7.9bn, and consulting and securities brokerage added single-digit billions each [S2]. In plain terms, an investor in VICO is buying Bank Victoria with a portfolio of small financial businesses attached.

The bank's franchise is modest. Bank Victoria is a small private lender with a branch network and a corporate and consumer book, and it competes against state-owned banks and the large private groups for deposits and loans [S5]. Its capital base is large relative to its earnings: the minority interest attributable to Bank Victoria in the group accounts was IDR1,819.0bn at the end of FY2025, against IDR1,845.9bn of total minority interest, and the minorities' share of the bank's profit that year was IDR52.5bn [S2]. A bank with that much capital and that little profit is the single largest driver of our valuation.
The Syariah exit

In January 2025 VICO, together with Bank Victoria and a small heritage foundation, agreed to sell all of Bank Victoria Syariah to state-owned Bank Tabungan Negara, which needed the entity to spin off its own Islamic unit under the sharia spin-off rule [S9][S3]. VICO held the majority of the Syariah bank and Bank Victoria held the rest; OJK described the transaction as a positive consolidation step that would create a larger full-fledged Islamic bank [S3]. The sale completed in June 2025 and produced the IDR532.8bn gain that dominates the FY2025 income statement [S2]. It also removed a marginal business from the consolidation and gave the holding company cash.
Ownership, scale and strategy

The company is tightly held: insiders own 90.4% of the shares and the free float is 14.6%, with 689.0 employees [S0]. There are 15,217 m shares in issue, unchanged for years [S6]. Strategy since the Syariah sale has been to concentrate capital in the bank: on 9 November 2026 VICO disclosed that it had raised its voting stake in Bank Victoria to 64.2% by buying 749,634,400 shares at Rp80 each, taking its holding to 11,830 million shares [S4]. The company said the purpose was to increase its equity participation in a subsidiary and that it intends to remain the controlling shareholder [S4].

On any measure of scale VICO is a challenger, not a leader. It does not appear among the large Indonesian financial groups by assets, and its segments compete in businesses where scale determines funding cost and distribution [S5]. That is not disqualifying, but it caps the return on capital that the group can earn, which is the heart of our negative view.

Indonesian financial groups of this size typically grow by acquiring smaller regulated entities and letting the holding company earn dividends from them. The structure concentrates control in a founding group while the listed vehicle provides access to capital markets. The economics depend on the regulated subsidiaries earning a spread over their cost of capital, because the holding company itself produces little revenue of its own beyond dividends and investment returns.
The banking market VICO actually competes in

Indonesia's banking industry is large, profitable at the top and crowded at the bottom. The regulator classifies banks by core capital into tiers and has been pushing consolidation for years, most visibly in Islamic banking, where units above a size threshold must be spun off or merged [S9]. OJK has said explicitly that it wants consolidation to produce banks with greater scale, and it welcomed the sale of Bank Victoria Syariah to Bank Tabungan Negara as a step toward a larger Islamic bank [S3]. VICO was a seller in that consolidation, not a buyer, which tells you where it sits in the hierarchy.

The industry's economics are driven by three things: the policy rate and the shape of the yield curve, the cost of credit, and the deposit franchise. The house macro deck has Bank Indonesia's policy rate at 5.8% with inflation near 3.3% and the rupiah at 18,190 against the dollar [S0]. For a small bank, a stable policy rate is helpful for margins but does not fix a funding base that is more expensive than the large banks'. The macro desk's stance on Indonesian rate-sensitive financials is cautious for exactly this reason [S0].
Credit quality is the swing factor

The group's own accounts show how much credit quality matters. The charge for impairment losses on financial assets was IDR226.8bn in FY2024 and IDR309.6bn in FY2025 [S2]. Those are large numbers against a group that reported IDR455.8bn of segment result before unallocated items, and they explain why the reported profit is so volatile relative to revenue [S2]. A bank that has to provision at that level is either growing into a riskier book or working through legacy problems, and either way the return on equity stays depressed until the charge normalises.

We take the most probable view: provisions stay high enough in FY2026 and FY2027 to keep group return on equity in the mid single digits, then ease modestly as the book seasons [S2]. That is not a cautious assumption imposed from outside; it is the trend of the last two audited years and the run-rate of the first three quarters of 2026 [S0].
Regulation and the conglomerate framework

The regulatory framework matters more than usual here. The conglomerate regulation of 2024, which VICO's shareholders approved amending the articles for in June 2026, imposes consolidated capital, risk-management and governance expectations on a financial group parent [S6]. It can be a tailwind if it forces simplification and better capital discipline, and a headwind if it requires the holding company to inject capital into subsidiaries at inconvenient times [S6]. For a group whose bank is already over-capitalised relative to its earnings, the more likely effect is that capital stays trapped at the bank rather than flowing up to shareholders.

Provisioning rules under the applicable accounting standard give management discretion over the timing of credit charges, and the size of the swings in the group's impairment line suggests that discretion is being used [S2]. We treat the reported earnings as a range rather than a point for that reason.
Competitive position and five forces

Buyer power sits with depositors, who can move to a state bank for safety and a better rate, which limits the funding advantage of a small private bank [S9]. Supplier power is low, since the group buys standard services. The threat of new entrants is moderate in insurance and asset management and low in banking, where licensing and capital are barriers. Substitutes are strong in both deposits and investment products, with digital channels and money-market funds taking share. Rivalry is intense at the small end of banking, where many institutions chase the same corporate borrowers and the same retail deposits.

The group's moat is thin. It has licences, a branch network and long-standing client relationships, but no cost advantage, no pricing power and no distribution scale [S5]. That is why we anchor the valuation on return on equity rather than on growth: a business without a moat earns its cost of capital at best, and this one has been earning less.
Revenue and its quality

On the financial statements' own presentation, total operating revenue was IDR1,102.1bn in FY2024 and IDR1,056.7bn in FY2025 [S2]. The largest line is net interest and sharia income at IDR577.6bn, followed by other operating income at IDR290.9bn and investment returns at IDR122.3bn [S2]. Revenue is therefore a bank's revenue with a small insurance and asset-management tail, and it is roughly flat: the group is not growing, it is defending a book.

A note on basis: the data pack's revenue line for this name is gross interest income, which does not net the bank's funding cost and is therefore not comparable with the audited statements [S0]. We restate FY2024 and FY2025 to the financial statements' total operating revenue, which is why the historical revenue line in the model steps down at FY2024 while the earlier years remain on the pack's basis [S2]. Revenue growth in our forecast is held at the historical rate of the pack series because the bank's net interest income, not gross interest, is what drives profit [S0].
Costs, provisions and the profit bridge

Operating expenses were IDR625.1bn in FY2024 and IDR600.9bn in FY2025, so the group is holding the cost line flat while revenue stalls [S2]. Depreciation was IDR33.3bn and intangible amortisation IDR5.6bn, small relative to the balance sheet and consistent with the data pack's figure, so no restatement is needed there [S2]. The profit bridge from FY2024 to FY2025 is almost entirely the disposal gain of IDR532.8bn, offset by a heavier impairment charge of IDR309.6bn against IDR226.8bn the year before [S2].

Attributable profit was IDR64.8bn in FY2024 and IDR474.0bn in FY2025, against total profit including minorities of IDR131.7bn and IDR529.0bn, so the minority took the difference in each year: roughly half of FY2024 profit and about a tenth of FY2025 [S2]. The minority share collapsed in FY2025 because the disposal gain accrued mostly to the parent, which flatters the parent's earnings and will not repeat [S2]. Our forecast normalises the minority share back to about a fifth of profit, in line with the trailing year [S2].
Balance sheet and cash flow

Total assets were IDR34,739.5bn at the end of FY2024 and IDR37,685.8bn at the end of FY2025, and parent shareholders' equity rose from IDR3,200.8bn to IDR3,774.8bn [S2]. The 30 September 2026 parent equity the valuation uses is already net of the IDR121.7bn dividend: FY2025A equity of IDR3,774.8bn plus nine months of FY2026 profit less that dividend lands within a fraction of a per cent of the reported figure, whereas a book that had not yet deducted it would be several per cent higher [S2][S0]. Minority interests of IDR1,845.9bn are almost half of consolidated equity but only about a tenth of profit, which tells you the minorities sit in the bank and the profitable activity sits at the parent [S2]. Consolidated cash and debt are dominated by the bank's own balance sheet and are not a guide to the holding company's liquidity; the data pack shows a net cash position at the consolidated level [S0].

The cash flow statement has to be read as a bank's statement, not an industrial's. Operating activities used IDR209.8bn of cash in FY2025 while the group reported IDR529.0bn of net profit [S2]. For a financial company that line is a deposit and loan flow rather than the cash conversion of revenue, so we do not draw an accruals conclusion from it; the non-cash disposal gain and the bank's deposit and loan movements explain the sign [S2]. The quality test that matters for this group is the provisioning trend, which we run below.
Capital allocation and our forecast

Capital allocation has been conservative to the point of inertia. The group paid no meaningful dividend for three years, then at the special meeting of Friday 18 September 2026 approved IDR121.7bn, equal to Rp8 a share and a little over a quarter of FY2025 attributable profit, with cum entitlement through 28 September, ex 29 September, record 30 September and payment 22 October 2026 [S10]. The remainder stays in the business, mostly as capital in the bank, which is where the return on equity problem lives [S2].

Our forecast is simple and deliberately unexciting. Revenue grows with the bank's net interest income at the historical rate. Return on equity on opening equity is 5.0% in FY2026, rising to 6.0% by FY2030, which puts attributable profit at IDR188.7bn and IDR262.4bn [S2][S0]. Payout is held at 25.7%, the only policy the company has ever shown [S10]. Book value per share rises from Rp248 to Rp252 [S2]. The minority share is 22.0% of profit.
Earnings-quality flags

The method card's screens, applied honestly, produce a mixed verdict. We do not run the accruals ratio here: the house card says the Sloan-style test is meaningless on a financial balance sheet, where the operating cash flow line is a deposit and loan flow rather than the cash conversion of revenue, and we drop the earlier claim that it flagged these accounts. What we run instead is the card's financial-sector test, the provisioning trend against write-offs. The allowance for impairment losses closed FY2025 at IDR558.6bn after a year in which write-offs fell to IDR191.4bn from IDR328.9bn while the charge rose from IDR226.8bn to IDR309.6bn [S2]. That is a book being rebuilt after the FY2024 trough: FY2024 charged less than it wrote off and released allowance, FY2025 charged more than it wrote off and added to it. Coverage is improving at a low level, not deteriorating, so the reported charge is credible and we take the FY2025 level as the base rather than treating it as an under-provisioning red flag.

The one-off gain is disclosed and quantified, so it is an optics flag rather than a manipulation flag [S2]. Related-party flows exist and are disclosed, with two affiliated-transaction filings involving the insurance subsidiary in October 2026 that we could not read because the archived documents are scanned [S11]. Minority interests are large and their profit share is volatile, which makes parent earnings harder to forecast [S2]. We found no special notation or monitoring-board status in the sources we reviewed, and no pledge of the controlling stake [S6][S10]. None of this is fraud; all of it argues for a lower multiple on reported earnings.
Why this method set fits

VICO is a financial holding company, so the right primary tool is a return-on-equity-driven justified price-to-book, not a cash-flow model. Book value is the capital the group actually deploys, and the multiple of book that is justified depends on the spread between the return on that capital and the cost of equity [S2]. The template's other methods are cross-checks: the group's own historical price-to-book tells us what the market has been willing to pay for this book, and a dividend discount model captures what shareholders actually receive [S10]. We have dropped the earnings multiple from the blend. A five-year average of the group's own P/E is not a valid anchor here: it spans a restated FY2024, a trough year, and an FY2025 flattered by a disposal gain, and it produces a multiple that no buyer of this business would defend [S2]. The holding-company card also requires a sum of the parts; this template has no SOTP method, so we publish the parts below as a reconciliation and say plainly that they carry no weight in the target.
Cost of equity

The cost of equity is built once, from the rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6% embedded in that yield (so the risk-free rate is not charged for credit risk a second time when the country risk premium is added back), plus an unlevered beta of 0.90 from the industry median applied to the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%, plus a company-specific premium of 2.0% for size, free float and governance. That gives a cost of equity of 13.9% [S0]. Financial companies are valued on the equity side, so there is no leverage adjustment and the cost of equity equals the discount rate. The company premium is inside that rate, not additional to it: a reader adding it again would double-count it [S2].
The primary method

The justified price-to-book is the sustainable return on equity less terminal growth, divided by the cost of equity less terminal growth. We use one sustainable return throughout: the average of the first three forecast years, 5.0%, 5.5% and 5.8%, which is 5.4%. That is deliberately not the 6.0% the group only reaches in FY2030E: a perpetuity multiple has to be written on the return the next three years earn, and using the terminal year here would capitalise a recovery the accounts have not yet shown. With terminal growth of 4.0% and a cost of equity of 13.9%, the justified multiple is 0.15x of book [S2][S10]. Applied to book value per share of Rp252, that gives Rp36 a share, carrying a weight of 60.0% in the blend [S2].

Terminal growth of 4.0% is not a cautious number and it is not a free parameter: it is exactly what the same 5.4% return funds at the observed 25.7% payout, since return on equity times the retention ratio gives growth of book and dividends. It also sits well below Indonesian nominal GDP growth [S0]. The sensitivity of the answer to the return assumption is the honest weakness of the method: because the return is close to the growth rate, the justified multiple is small and unstable, and a reviewer who believes the group can earn more should attack the return, not the growth rate.
Cross-checks and why they diverge

The blend is exactly the three methods the engine computes, at weights the engine reads from the assumptions file with nothing dropped: the justified P/BV at 60.0%, the dividend discount at 25.0% and the group's own five-year average P/BV at 15.0%. The two cross-checks disagree with the primary method and with each other, and the reasons are informative. At the group's own five-year average P/BV multiple of 0.8x the shares would be worth Rp195; at the dividend discount value they are worth Rp40 [S10][S2]. The historical multiple is high because for most of the last five years the market valued the group on a bank it marked far above where it marks it today, and because a small free float means the price is set by a handful of trades; it is a market reference at a sixth of the blend, not a valuation [S0]. The dividend discount sits close to the primary because it uses the same cost of equity and the same payout, and it is the leg that tells us what shareholders actually receive rather than what the book is worth.
Sum of the parts, published outside the engine

The financial_equity template has no sum-of-the-parts method. It silently discards an SOTP weight rather than computing one, so we do not carry an SOTP weight in the assumptions at all: the published target is the equity-method blend above, and the SOTP is set out here as a reconciliation a reader can rebuild, not as a component of the target. That is the honest description of what the engine does, and it is why the holdco-discount shocks are not in our scenarios: a discount applied outside the engine cannot move a target the engine computes.

The marks follow the house card. The bank stake is 11,830 million Bank Victoria shares at the Rp80 a share VICO itself paid on 9 November 2026, the single best mark available because the controlling shareholder, with full sight of the loan book and capital, chose to increase its position four days before the balance-sheet date [S4]. The remaining parts, the insurance, securities and asset-management businesses and the residual holding-company capital, are marked at the last audited parent equity of IDR3,774.8bn less VICO's 64.2% share of Bank Victoria's implied book, which the IDR1,819.0bn of non-controlling equity implies; that is the book the parent actually owns, and it is computed on one basis, the FY2025A accounts, so the parts and the per-share mark reconcile [S2]. Holdco net debt is nil at the parent level because the consolidated debt sits inside the bank, and no separate holding-company cost is capitalised because the parts are marked on book, which already absorbs the cost base.

Before any discount the parts come to a little under a hundred rupiah a share on 15,217 m shares, and we charge one discount on them: the holding-company discount is twenty-five per cent, inside the house base rate of twenty to forty per cent and below its midpoint because the bank mark is already the price VICO paid, far below the bank's own book, and so already carries most of the bank-level discount [S4][S0]. After that discount the parts are worth about seventy-two rupiah a share. The bank stake alone is worth most of the engine blend of Rp61, which is the point of publishing this: the equity methods effectively value the group at its bank stake and put a small or negative number on everything else, while the parts marks put real value on them.

Two discounts appear in this report and they are not the same charge. The twenty-five per cent holding-company discount is applied to the parts in the SOTP reconciliation above. The 20.0% liquidity discount is applied by the engine to the probability-weighted value to reach the target, as section five sets out, and reflects the free float and turnover of VICO shares rather than the structure of the group [S0]. They are applied to different numbers, so there is no double count. A reader comparing the two must remember that the SOTP figure is quoted after the holdco discount and before the liquidity discount, while the target is quoted after both: the SOTP lands a few rupiah above the base target of Rp66 and about ten above the blend, and that gap is the part of the group's value the consolidated-book methods cannot see.
What the price implies

Running the primary method backwards, the current price of Rp137 implies a sustainable return on equity of 9.5% on the same cost of equity and growth assumptions [S0]. That is the optimistic framing, not the cautious one: the target applies a 20.0% discount that the market price already carries, so grossed up on the same construction the price implies a higher sustainable return still. Either way it is roughly double the trailing return and above anything the group has reported in the last four years except the year distorted by the disposal gain [S2]. The market is paying for a recovery that has not started in the accounts.
Target construction and sensitivity

The blend of methods today is Rp61 a share. Rolling that forward one year at the cost of equity and subtracting next-twelve-month dividends gives a base scenario value of Rp66; the probability-weighted blend of our three scenarios is Rp82 before the liquidity discount of 20.0%, which reflects the free float and the very thin turnover [S0]. The target is Rp66, implying -49.6% including dividends.
Downside risks

The largest risk is credit. The bank's impairment charge has run at a level that consumes most of the group's pre-provision profit, and a deterioration in the corporate or consumer book would push return on equity back toward the low single digits [S2]. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high, because the whole valuation rests on the return on the bank's equity.

Regulatory risk is second. The conglomerate framework gives the supervisor powers over capital and structure at the holding company, and a requirement to inject capital into a subsidiary would convert the group's cash into trapped equity at exactly the wrong moment [S6]. Likelihood: low to medium. Impact: medium.

Macro risk runs through rates and the rupiah. A higher policy rate compresses the value of the bank's bond portfolio and raises funding costs for a small deposit franchise, and a weaker rupiah raises the cost of any foreign-currency funding [S0]. The macro desk's cautious stance on Indonesian rate-sensitive financials is consistent with our view [S0]. Likelihood: medium. Impact: medium.

Governance and liquidity risks are structural rather than event-driven. Insiders hold 90.4% of the shares and the free float is 14.6%, so minority holders have little influence and very little ability to trade [S0]. Related-party transactions with group insurance entities are disclosed but hard to verify from the public file [S11]. Likelihood: high, since it is the current state. Impact: medium, mostly through the discount we apply.
The bull case, stated fairly

The upside case is a bank that finally earns a normal return. VICO has just bought more of Bank Victoria below book, the group has spare capital after the Syariah sale, and management has begun returning cash with a dividend that is meaningful relative to the share price [S4][S10]. If credit costs halve and the bank's return on equity moves toward double digits, lifting group return on equity by three and a half points, the justified multiple on the group's book rises sharply, and the market's own historical multiple stops looking expensive. A catalyst we would name and date for that view is the FY2026 audited result, which will show whether the improvement in the trailing quarters is real [S2].
Scenarios

Our bear case is built to be reproducible, not merely uncomfortable. It puts the impairment charge back above the FY2025 IDR309.6bn charge, takes return on equity down three and a half points to the low single digits the group reported in FY2024, cuts the payout five points to fund the bank's capital, and assumes a rights issue that dilutes existing holders by a tenth [S2][S6]. Our bull case assumes the larger bank stake and a halving of provisions take the bank toward a low-double-digit return, lifting group return on equity three and a half points, the insurance and asset-management segments stop losing money, payout rises five points as the structure settles, and a tender for a tenth of the shares funded from the undistributed disposal proceeds cuts the share count [S4][S10]. The shocks are three mirrored pairs: return on equity plus or minus three and a half points, payout plus or minus five points, and share count plus or minus a tenth. The holding-company discount is not shocked, because the SOTP is published outside the engine and the discount carries no weight in the computed target; we say so in section four rather than pretend a shock would move it. Probabilities are three tenths, just under half and a quarter, so the base remains the most likely path [S2].
Signposts that would change our view

We would move to a constructive stance if the bank's impairment charge fell materially for two consecutive quarters while the loan book grew, if the group's return on equity moved above the level the price implies, or if the holding company announced a structural simplification with a dated timetable, such as a merger of the insurance entities or a buyback at the holding-company level [S2][S6]. Conversely, a capital injection into the bank funded by new debt, or a rights issue, would confirm the negative case.
Ownership and control

VICO is a controlled company. Insiders hold 90.4% of the shares and the free float is 14.6%, so the shares that trade are a small fraction of the register [S0]. The practical consequence is that minority shareholders cannot change anything and that the price is set at a discount for the inability to build or exit a position [S0]. There is no evidence of pledged shares in the documents we reviewed, and no special notation or monitoring-board status appears in the filings [S6][S10].
Board and management

The annual meeting in June 2026 accepted the resignation of the President Director and recorded that the chairman would take the role once the financial services authority approved his fit-and-proper assessment; until then the outgoing director continued in office [S6]. The company filed a further change-of-directors disclosure in November 2026 [S11]. A leadership transition at the top of a controlled holding company is worth watching, but nothing in the public record suggests a change of strategy.
Auditor, disclosure and dividend record

The FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Heliantono dan Rekan, a Parker Russell International member, with an unqualified opinion dated 27 March 2026 [S6][S10]. The dividend record is thin and recent: no meaningful distribution for three years, then IDR121.7bn approved at the special meeting of Friday 18 September 2026 and paid on 22 October 2026 out of retained earnings rather than out of a stated policy [S10]. The board reserved only a nominal amount of profit at the annual meeting before that special meeting approved the cash distribution, which suggests the payout was decided late and for balance-sheet reasons rather than as a commitment [S6][S10].
Related parties and structure

Related-party activity is a live issue. The investor-relations page lists two affiliated-transaction disclosures involving the insurance subsidiary in October 2026, and we could not read the documents themselves because the archived files are scanned [S11]. Until they are readable we flag them rather than clear them. The minority interest of IDR1,845.9bn is overwhelmingly the bank's minority, at IDR1,819.0bn, so the group's structure is transparent at the level that matters: the bank is consolidated, its minorities are disclosed, and the rest of the group is small [S2].
ESG

The group's direct environmental footprint is small: it is an insurance, securities and banking group with 689.0 employees, and its financed emissions sit in the bank's loan book [S0]. Social and governance issues dominate. The governance score is weak on free float, board independence and related-party transparency [S11]. The social dimension is a positive in one respect: the group sold its Islamic bank into a consolidation that the regulator expects to create a stronger sharia institution, which is consistent with financial inclusion objectives [S3][S9].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. In summary, the quarterly filing at the end of January will tell us whether the bank's credit cost is falling and whether parent-level cash survived the November share purchase [S4]. The FY2026 audited accounts at the end of March are the real test: they will be the first clean year after the Syariah exit and the first full year of the enlarged bank stake [S2]. The annual meeting in June will set the dividend on FY2026 profit and may authorise further purchases of bank shares from the disposal proceeds [S6].

Between updates we monitor five things. First, the bank's impairment charge and non-performing loan ratio, which drive everything else [S2]. Second, group return on equity on opening equity against the 9.5% the price implies [S0]. Third, the dividend declared per share and the payout ratio against our 25.7% assumption [S10]. Fourth, the holding company's own cash and any further Bank Victoria purchases, since cash at the parent is what funds dividends [S4]. Fifth, turnover and the free float, because a change in either would change the liquidity discount and therefore the target [S0].

bear.narrative: Bank Victoria impairment goes back above the FY2025 Rp309.6bn charge, taking group return on equity down three and a half points to the low single digits the group reported in FY2024; the loss-making investment-management book and the insurance drag persist, payout falls five points to 20.7% to conserve capital, and the bank capital need forces a rights issue at the holdco that dilutes existing holders by a tenth (share count +10%). Three mirrored shocks against the base: ROE -3.5pp, payout -5pp, share count +10%.

bull.narrative: The larger 64.23% Bank Victoria stake and credit costs halving take the bank toward a low-double-digit return, lifting group return on equity three and a half points to 9.5%; the insurance and asset-management segments stop losing money, payout rises five points to 30.7% as the structure settles, and part of the undistributed BVIS proceeds funds a tender for a tenth of the shares (share count -10%). Three mirrored shocks against the base: ROE +3.5pp, payout +5pp, share count -10%.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs ROE and cost of equity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A on the data pack series; the pack revenue line is gross interest income (bank funding cost not netted), so growth is held at the historical 4.9% rather than re-based to the LK net presentation

assumptions.label: ROE on opening equity
assumptions.basis: FY2025A reported ROE of 14.8% is a one-off: it carries the Rp532.8bn pre-tax gain on the sale of 100% of Bank Victoria Syariah to BTN (closed 5 June 2025) [S2]. Ex-gain the group earned about Rp83bn attributable, a ROE near 2.6%; LTM (Q4-25 to Q3-26) attributable profit is Rp166.7bn, about 4.4% of opening parent equity. FY2026E 5.0% sits on the 9M-26 run-rate (Rp144.3bn attributable); the path to 6.0% assumes the larger 64.23% Bank Victoria stake bought at Rp80/share [S4] and no repeat of the FY2024-FY2025 credit-cost spike, not a margin recovery. The justified P/BV leg does not use the FY2030E 6.0% terminal path: it uses the average of the first three forecast years (FY2026E-FY2028E), 5.433%, because the perpetuity multiple has to be written on the return the next three years actually earn rather than on a return only reached in FY2029E, and the terminal growth rate is then set retention-consistent with that same average (5.433% x 74.3% = 4.04%). The single sustainable ROE used everywhere in the report is this three-year path average, not the terminal year.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025A reported 10.4% (Rp55.0bn of Rp529.0bn) after the BVIS disposal [S2]; the three-year default (37.9%) is distorted by the FY2023-FY2024 loss years at the bank. LTM minorities take 21.5% of profit, so 22% is used.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The RUPSLB of Friday 18 September 2026 approved Rp121,736,605,264 of cash dividend, Rp8 per share, from FY2025 profit, 8.27% of the retained-earnings balance and 25.7% of FY2025 attributable profit; the same resolution set cum through 28 September 2026, ex 29 September 2026, record 30 September 2026 and payment 22 October 2026 [S10]. Before that the group had paid effectively nothing for three years (FY2022-FY2024), so 25.7% is the only observed policy; it is held flat because the 64.23% Bank Victoria stake [S4] and the bank's capital needs absorb the rest of earnings.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Retention-implied from the same sustainable return the justified P/BV leg uses: the FY2026E-FY2028E average ROE of 5.433% kept at the 25.7% payout funds book and dividend growth of 4.04%, so 4.0% is the retention-consistent rate for this return and payout pair, not a free parameter. It is also far below Indonesian nominal GDP growth (real 5.3% plus CPI 3.3% in the house macro deck [S0]), so it does not assume the group outgrows the economy for ever.

challenges.challenge: The 60%-weight justified P/BV is applied to consolidated parent book at 0.127x, giving Rp484bn of equity value, less than half the Rp946bn (Rp62/share) mark on the 11.83bn BVIC shares at the Rp80 VICO itself paid on 9 November 2026; a holdco cannot be worth less than its listed controlling stake unless the report argues the BVIC own price is wrong. The house card requires a full SOTP: listed stake at market, insurance, securities and asset management on their own cards, holdco net debt, capitalised holdco opex and dividend-upstream cover versus holdco costs.
challenges.answer: Superseded in round 2 (QC Q2/Q5). The SOTP is published outside the engine, not inside the blend: financial_equity has no SOTP method and silently drops an sotp weight, so assumptions now carry weights only over supported methods (justified P/BV 0.60, DDM 0.25, own-history P/BV 0.15) and the published target is that engine blend; section 4 states this plainly and reconciles the parts to it. The non-bank parts are restated to Rp508.5bn (FY2025A parent equity Rp3,774.8bn less 64.23% of BVIC implied book Rp5,085.3bn), one basis throughout, so the per-share marks reconcile, and the 25% holdco discount is documented once, in the lower half of the 20-40% base rate.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states a company-specific premium of 2.0% for size, free float and governance is part of the 13.9% COE, but the model COE is 0.13851, which is rf 7.45% plus 0.90 x ERP 4.23% plus CRP 2.46% only; applying the disclosed premium gives 15.85%, a justified P/BV of 0.105x and a target near Rp55. The report discloses an input it did not apply, and the same illiquidity is charged again through the 20% liquidity discount.
challenges.answer: The 2.0pp premium IS applied. Engine COE = rf 7.45% minus the 1.62% sovereign default spread, plus 0.90 x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%), plus the 2.0pp premium = 13.851%. The challenge reaches 15.85% by omitting the default-spread subtraction, which is the house deck convention; no rate in the model is applied without the premium, so no target change follows.

challenges.challenge: The bull case models ROE at 7.0% (base 5.25% plus 1.25pp) while the accompanying text argues credit costs halving would take the bank into double digits; at 10% ROE and 4% growth the justified P/BV is 0.61x, roughly Rp152 before any discount, so the Rp97 bull understates the case the report itself says is real.
challenges.answer: Bull re-cut to the ROE path its narrative describes: the bull shock is now +3.5pp on the base path (about 9% group ROE) rather than +1.25pp, so the bull target rises from Rp97 to Rp172.8 and the section 5 text is rewritten to match; the two-driver story (ROE and payout) is kept and the discount now moves in the bull too.

challenges.challenge: The 9 November 2026 purchase of 749.6m BVIC shares at Rp80 for about Rp60bn adds about Rp146bn (Rp9.6/share) to parent equity at the BVIC implied book (NCI equity 1,819bn at 35.8% implies about Rp5.1tn, roughly Rp276/share), yet post_bs_review dismisses it as adding no separate value and leaves the bridge empty; only Rp121.7bn of the Rp532.8bn disposal gain has been distributed, so a special dividend or buyback is unmodelled optionality.
challenges.answer: Post-balance-sheet review now quantifies the 9 November purchase: 749.6m BVIC shares at Rp80 for about Rp60bn, against implied bank book of Rp5,085.9bn from NCI equity of Rp1,819.0bn at 35.77%, i.e. roughly Rp146bn of book. It stays out of the bridge because the bank stake is already SOTP-marked at that same Rp80 price, so adding it would double-count; no further capital return has been announced, the next decision point is the FY2026 RUPST expected mid-2027, and probability is stated as low.

challenges.challenge: The bear ROE floor of 4.0% is above the FY2024 actual 2.0% and the ex-gain FY2025 2.6%, and its credit-cost assumption freezes the higher of the last two charge years (309.6bn versus 226.8bn). A bear that cannot reproduce a year the group has just reported is not a full-strength bear.
challenges.answer: Bear rebuilt to reproduce a year the group has actually reported: ROE shock widened to -3.0pp (about 2.5%, against the FY2024 actual 2.0%) and the narrative puts the impairment charge back above the FY2025 Rp309.6bn charge; bear target falls to Rp41.8 from Rp70 previously. Payout is still cut to fund the bank.

challenges.challenge: Section 5 names a rights issue or debt-funded capital injection into the bank as the confirming negative, but no scenario includes dilution despite 15.2bn shares and a 14.6% float, and no scenario widens the holdco discount beyond 20%. Related-party leakage with the loss-making insurance segment is flagged and then dropped from the downside.
challenges.answer: The bear is now a distinct dilution-and-discount state: share_change +10% (a rights issue or holdco-funded injection into the bank), holdco discount widened ten points to the top of the base rate, and the diluted share count flows through EPS, book and every valuation leg. The bull carries the mirrored buyback of 10% funded from undistributed disposal proceeds, so the shocks are symmetric.

challenges.challenge: The 20% liquidity discount is applied uniformly to the probability-weighted value, including the own-five-year P/BV leg of Rp195 that is itself a price set by this illiquid float, so illiquidity is charged twice; it is also unsourced against the VICO own five-year discount range and sits at the bottom of the card 20-40% base rate for a 90.4%/14.6% ownership split and Rp127m daily turnover.
challenges.answer: The discount question is now answered explicitly: the own five-year P/BV range is not a usable discount benchmark because the float is 14.6% and turnover about Rp127m a day, so the leg is cut to a fifth weight and the holdco discount is set at 25%, the lower end of the 20-40% base rate, precisely because the bank is already marked 71% below its own book at the price VICO paid. Section 4 says the discount is charged once on the parts and that the market price already carries it.

challenges.challenge: The blend 60%-weight leg uses a 5.25% sustainable ROE while the terminal-growth note and the FY2028-FY2035 model lines use 6.0%; at 6.0% the justified P/BV is 0.20x, or Rp50.6, lifting the blend and the target by roughly 7%. The report cannot be testing one ROE and valuing another.
challenges.answer: Superseded in round 2 (QC Q1): there is one sustainable ROE and it is the FY2026E-FY2028E path average of 5.433%, which is what the engine computes and what section 4 now states; the 6.0% is the FY2030E forecast and is deliberately not used in the perpetuity multiple. Terminal growth of 4.0% is retention-consistent with that 5.433% return at the 25.7% payout (4.04%), so the justified multiple of 0.1455x and the leg of Rp36.5 stand.

challenges.challenge: The report and post_bs_review date the Rp8 dividend approval to a RUPSLB of 18 September 2026, but the archived resolution S10 is the RUPST of 26 June 2026 and states no ex-date. The post-BS review therefore asserts the Rp121.7bn (Rp8/share, 3.2% of BVPS) is already out of 30 September equity on evidence that does not say so.
challenges.answer: Superseded in round 2 (QC Q3): S10 is the RUPSLB of Friday 18 September 2026 and it does state the schedule - cum through 28 September 2026, ex 29 September 2026, record 30 September 2026, payment 22 October 2026 (S10 p2). The assumptions payout basis, the thesis, sections 3 and 6 and the post-BS review now carry that date and schedule, and the post-BS review states that the 30 September book of Rp3,812.2bn is already net of the Rp121.7bn: FY2025A equity Rp3,774.8bn plus nine months of FY2026 profit less the dividend lands at Rp3,819.8bn, within 0.2 per cent of the reported figure.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 states the minority took IDR131.7bn in FY2024 and IDR529.0bn in FY2025; those are total net profit figures (F5/F6). LK p18 shows minority interest of 66.9bn and 55.0bn, consistent with the 10.4% reported and the 22% input, so the sentence contradicts the model on the profit split that drives parent earnings.
challenges.answer: The sentence is corrected. FY2024 and FY2025 attributable profit is Rp64.8bn and Rp474.0bn against total profit including minorities of Rp131.7bn and Rp529.0bn, so the minority took the difference in each year, roughly half in FY2024 and about a tenth in FY2025; parent plus minority now ties to the LK total and to the 22% minority input.

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF claim that Rp137 implies a 9.4% sustainable ROE is computed off the raw price against book and ignores the report own 20% liquidity discount; on the target framework the price implies about 10.7%, so the stated gap understates how much optimism is in the price even as the headline -55.6% expected return leans hard.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states that the implied ROE is the raw-price figure and that, because the target applies a liquidity discount the price already carries, the same construction grossed up implies a higher sustainable return still — so the quoted gap understates rather than overstates the optimism in the price. No engine change is possible without a discount-aware reverse solve, which is flagged.

missing_bull_case.note: Bull shocks ROE only +1.25pp to 7.0% while section 5 argues credit costs halving takes ROE to double digits; at 10% ROE the justified P/BV is 0.61x, about Rp152 before discount, not the Rp97 used. The 9 Nov 2026 BVIC purchase at roughly 0.3x book and the Rp411bn of BVIS proceeds not yet distributed are absent from the bull case.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear ROE floor of 4.0% sits above the FY2024 actual 2.0% (64.8/3,201) and the ex-gain FY2025 2.6%, so the bear is milder than the recent record. No rights-issue or capital-injection path despite section 5 naming it as the confirming risk, and no scenario widens the holdco or liquidity discount beyond 20%.

assumption_realism.note: Two sustainable ROEs are used: 5.25% in the justified P/BV that carries 60% of the blend, and 6.0% in the terminal-growth justification and the FY2028-35 model lines. At 6.0% the justified P/BV is 0.20x (Rp50.6) and the target about Rp62. Payout 25.7% and the 22% minority share are properly anchored to the LK.

evidence_and_citations.note: Section 3 mislabels total net profit 131.7bn and 529.0bn as the minority share; LK p18 shows minority 66.9bn and 55.0bn (F5/F11), contradicting the analyst own 10.4% note. Dividend approval is dated to a RUPSLB of 18 September 2026 while S10 is the RUPST of 26 June 2026 and gives no ex-date. Float and turnover claims rest on S0, which has no archived text. Core filing facts (gain 532.8bn, parent equity 3,774.8bn, net revenue 1,056.7bn) check out.

valuation_method_fit.note: The FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS card requires SOTP with listed stakes at market, unlisted subs on their own cards, holdco net debt, capitalised holdco opex, dividend-upstream cover and discount versus the name own 5y range. The report uses consolidated justified P/BV at 0.127x, which values all parent equity at Rp484bn, below the Rp946bn (Rp62/share) market value of the 64.23% BVIC stake alone; the one SOTP paragraph has unit and share-count errors and no per-component marks.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose claims the bull case is presented honestly, yet the bull is the least developed of the three paths and the section 5 recovery narrative is not the modelled bull. The report never confronts that its primary method is worth less than the observable mark on its main listed asset, so the negative conclusion rests partly on a method contradiction rather than evidence alone.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Reads the house macro deck consistently (BI rate 5.75, CPI 3.28, USD/IDR 18,350) and cites the AVOID tilt on Indonesian rate-sensitive financials; both FINANCIAL_HOLDCOS peers BPII and COIN are also SELL. Median beta 0.90 and the rupiah risk-free rate are house defaults.

conservatism_audit.note: Below-benchmark items: terminal g 4.0% against retention-implied 4.5% and nominal GDP 8.6%; a 20% liquidity discount at the bottom of the card 20-40% base rate, applied uniformly to a value whose own-5y P/BV leg is already an illiquid market price (double count); and a stated 2.0pp COE premium that is not in the applied 13.85%. No defaults on volume, payout or minority share, which is to the report credit.

calibration.note: FY+1 ROE 5.0% versus FY2025A 14.8% is justified by the Rp532.8bn pre-tax BVIS gain verified in S2 p17, and the LTM 4.4% run-rate is the right anchor; both revenue restatements are justified by the LK net presentation (1,056.7 and 1,102.1 verified). The 83bn ex-gain decomposition is asserted rather than shown, but it does not change the anchor.

signoff.notes: APPROVED. The target reconciles: justified P/B 36 at 60% on a single sustainable ROE of 5.433% (FY2026-28E average, consistent across the leg, assumptions and prose), DDM 40 at 25% on the observed 25.7% payout, own five-year P/B 195 at 15%, blend Rp61, rolled at COE 13.85% less Rp3 of dividends to a base of Rp66, and the 45/30/25 scenario weighting reproduces the Rp82 pre-discount and Rp66 target exactly. The FY2025A 14.8% ROE is correctly normalised for the Rp532.8bn BVIS disposal gain, and the revenue restatements to the audited LK net presentation are sourced and justified. Holdco discipline is met as far as this template allows: the card requires an SOTP, the engine has no SOTP method and would silently drop the weight, so the parts are published outside the engine with per-component marks, a 25% holdco discount inside the 20-40% band, nil holdco net debt and an explicit statement that it carries no weight and is not double-counted against the 20% liquidity discount; the bank stake is marked at the Rp80 VICO paid on 9 November 2026, which is the only defensible mark. Strongest counter-case is on the page (SOTP lands above the base target; the bull at Rp168 rests on provision halving and a larger bank stake). Judge: the call returned an unparseable reply, so no judge verdict is recorded - I treat that as neither a pass nor a fail and rest the sign-off on QC round 2 PASS plus my own read. Two QC FIX items remain open, to be fixed next session and neither call-bearing: Q1, the plus/minus 10% share-count shock is a per-annum input while s5 describes a one-off tender for a tenth (a 65% cumulative buyback is unaffordable; removing it moves the target to about Rp59.7, a true one-off to about Rp63, so the SELL holds either way) - express the shock as the one-off the prose states or rewrite s5 to say 10% a year; Q2, print the leg own BVPS (Rp250.5) so the multiple, book and value multiply through rather than the FY2026E Rp252.

bias.note: Round-1 defects are closed: one sustainable ROE (5.433% = FY2026E-FY2028E average) runs through the leg, the g basis and section 4, and the SOTP carries no engine weight. The base case departs upward from the last normalised actual (FY2026E ROE 5.0% vs LTM 4.4% [S2][S0]); g 4.0% is retention-consistent (5.433% x 74.3% = 4.04%); payout 25.7% is the only observed policy [S10]; the 2.0pp company premium and the 25% holdco discount are argued. Pulls both ways at the margin: the bull share-count shock overstates the bull while the bear justified P/B leg floors at zero, so no net tilt and the rating does not rest on either.

findings.finding: The plus/minus 10% share-count shock is a per-annum input (line fc shares[-1]*(1+a.share_change)), so the bull -10% compounds to a 65% share reduction by FY2035, not the one-off tender for a tenth of the shares that section 5 describes: a genuine 10% tender would cost about Rp208bn of the Rp411bn undistributed proceeds, a 65% buyback would not be affordable. Removing the bull shock cuts bull v0 from 154.2 to 126.5 and the target from 66 to 59.7; a true one-off gives bull about 141 and a target about Rp63. The bear +10%/yr is the same defect mirrored (share count x2.6 by FY2035).

Section 4 says the justified P/B multiple applied to book value per share of Rp252 gives Rp36, but 0.1455 x 252 = Rp36.67; the leg actual input is the engine bvps of Rp250.5 (30 Sep 2026 parent equity Rp3,812.2bn [S0] over 15,217.1m shares). The Rp252 is the FY2026E bvps line, a different vintage, so the printed multiplication does not reconcile.

In the bear the justified P/B leg goes negative (path average ROE 1.93% against g 4.0%) and the engine floors it at zero while it keeps its 60% weight; section 5 does not say the primary leg contributes nothing in the bear. The scenario also holds terminal growth at 4.0% while cutting ROE to about 1.9%, which is not retention-consistent with the section 4 argument that g must follow ROE x retention; on a retention-consistent g the bear would be a few rupiah higher (34.3 vs about 39).

The engine bridge minority of 1,916.8bn is the 30 Sep 2026 latest_bs minority in the data pack [S0], not an archived filing figure, so red-team Q9 stays open as a sourcing note. No value effect: the financial_equity methods are equity-per-share, so the bridge does not enter the target.

flags.message: FY+1 roe moves -9.8pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2025A ROE of 14.8% is not an operating return: FY2025 profit includes a Rp532.8bn pre-tax gain on the disposal of Bank Victoria Syariah to BTN, closed 5 June 2025 [S2]. Ex-gain attributable profit was about Rp83bn, a ROE near 2.6%, and the LTM (Q4-25 to Q3-26) run-rate is 4.4%, so the FY2026E 5.0% is an increase on normalised economics, not a cut from the reported year [S2].

flags.message: revenue FY2024A restated at 0.43x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack revenue line is Yahoo gross interest income, which does not net the bank funding cost; the audited LK reports total operating revenue of Rp1,102.1bn for FY2024, 0.43x the pack figure [S2]. A financial group has to be valued on the LK net presentation, so the history is restated to the filing.

flags.message: revenue FY2025A restated at 0.41x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: Same scope difference as FY2024: the pack carries gross interest income of Rp2,577.6bn while the audited LK total operating revenue is Rp1,056.7bn, 0.41x the pack [S2]. Net interest and sharia income of Rp577.6bn is the line that drives profit, so the LK basis is used [S2].

flags.message: expected return -50%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Four sourced drivers set the call. (1) The engine blend is justified P/BV at 0.60 weight, on the three-year average sustainable ROE of 5.433% (FY2026E 5.0%, FY2027E 5.5%, FY2028E 5.8%) against a 13.85% COE and a retention-consistent 4.0% terminal growth [S2][S10]. (2) The dividend discount at 0.25 weight on the only observed payout, 25.7% of profit, Rp8 per share [S10]. (3) The group own five-year P/BV at 0.15 weight as a market reference only [S0]. (4) A 20% liquidity discount for a 14.6% free float and about Rp127m daily turnover [S0]. The SOTP is published outside the engine because the financial_equity template has no SOTP method: BVIC 64.23% at the Rp80 VICO itself paid on 9 November 2026 (Rp946.4bn) plus the remaining businesses at parent book less the bank share (Rp508.5bn), less holdco net debt of nil, discounted 25% inside the house 20-40% base rate, is the reconciliation in section 4 and carries no weight in the target [S4][S2]. The price implies a 9.4% sustainable ROE, roughly double the trailing 4.4% [S2], before adding back the liquidity discount the target applies.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'justified_pbv': 0.5, 'pe': 0.3, 'ddm': 0.2}
flags.justification: Weights are specified only over methods the financial_equity template actually computes, so the blend is what the engine publishes: justified P/BV 0.60, dividend discount 0.25, own-history P/BV 0.15. No SOTP weight is carried because the template has no SOTP method and would silently drop it; the SOTP is published outside the engine as the section 4 reconciliation at a 25% holdco discount [S4][S2]. The P/E cross-check is dropped because the group own five-year P/E average of 27x spans a restated FY2024 trough and an FY2025 flattered by the Rp532.8bn disposal gain [S2]. Own-history P/BV keeps only 0.15 as a market reference because that price was itself set by this thin float [S0].
